newsitem.title: USA: Compaq to cut memory prices on its PC lines.
newsitem.headline: Compaq to cut memory prices on its PC lines.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp., the world's largest seller of personal computers, Monday cut prices on the computer memory chip modules it sells to run within its desktop, portable and server computer lines by up to 65 percent.
The price cuts were part of Compaq's new logistics programme designed to cut the time between when a customer places an order and a product is delivered to less than 48 hours.
The "Sterling Memory Initiative" will allow Compaq to rapidly respond to falling component prices and rival pricing actions, it said.
It will be implemented in Canada in the fourth quarter and in stages in the rest of the world in the first quarter of 1997.
Houston-based Compaq cut prices for most of its computer memory modules, which come in a range of speeds and layouts, by 35 percent to 45 percent.

As part of the plan, Compaq said it will now hold raw Dynamic Random Access Memory chips in inventory and assemble these key computer memories into specific product modules the day an order is received.
Based on the improved availability and reduced inventory resulting from the build-to-order process, Compaq said it is able to respond immediately to component and competitive.
Compaq said it purchases memory exclusively from vendors that meet the computermaker's quality standards.
Compaq's stock rose 87.5 cents to $67.25 early on the New York Stock Exchange.
